newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's rosy picture marred by attacks on poll plan.
newsitem.headline: HK's rosy picture marred by attacks on poll plan.

text.p: Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa on Thursday marked the end of the territory's first month under Chinese rule, painting a with a rosy picture of life in the former British colony.
But he ran into criticism from democrats, human rights and union activists angry at proposed arrangements for legislative elections due next year.
Speaking at a lunch for businessmen, Tung said life had not changed in Hong Kong, which remained a free market economy where the rule of law reigned.
People were free to express their political views and had kept their rights and freedoms as guaranteed by the new constitution, the Basic Law, he said.
Hong Kong reverted to Beijing's control on July 1 after 156 years of British colonial rule.
This week a Hong Kong appeal court crushed a challenge to the legality of the unelected provisional legislature installed by Beijing, averting a potential constitutional crisis.
Tung said the challenge showed that "the rule of law is of paramount importance to Hong Kong", and he expected the courts would soon hear more challenges to the legislative system.

After the handover, China scrapped Hong Kong's elected colonial legislature and replaced it with the Beijing-appointed provisional legislative chamber which will operate until a new legislature is elected next year.

But on the last day of an exercise launched by Tung last week to consult the public on planned arrangements for the 1998 election, democrats, human rights activists and unionists slammed his proposals as not fair, open or democratic.
Under the plan, half the 60 seats of the new legislature will be filled by representatives from business and professional bodies called functional constitutencies.
Twenty seats are to be returned by geographical constitutencies in direct elections and 10 by an election committee made up of businessmen and professionals.
The Democratic Party and the Hong Kong Human Rights Monitor group said the proposal to give votes in functional constituencies to corporations rather than individuals was a roll-back of democracy.

For functional constituencies, more than two million people who were eligible to vote in the 1995 Legislative Council polls would be disenfranchised under Tung's plan. They would be replaced by corporate votes totalling no more than 10,000.
Leading unionist Lee Cheuk-yan complained that the change would give more powers to the business sector.
Democratic Party chairman Martin Lee also criticised a proposal for Hong Kong to be divided into five geographical constituencies, each with multiple seats.
At the last legislative election in 1995, the territory was split into 20 smaller constituencies, each with a single seat.
Lee claimed the new plan aimed at reducing the chance of victory for the Democatic Party, which won the largest number of seats in the 1995 polls.

During the Democratic Party's first meeting with Tung since the handover, Lee urged Tung to help party members gain entry permits into China. Beijing had turned down some members's applications to renew their China entry permits, and confiscated the entry permits of three others, he said.
A spokeswoman for Tung said the leader noted Lee's request and urged democrats to learn more about China.
On Thursday, a score of pro-democracy activists protested outside the Hong Kong office of China's Foreign Ministry to demand the release of jailed Chinese dissidents.
